chunks: My father, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated to us, saying: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to us, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Isbahani, from al-Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Manqari, who said: Fudayl ibn 'Iyad narrated to us, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), saying:

I asked him about the greater pilgrimage, so he said: Do you have anything about it? I said: Yes. Ibn Abbas used to say: The greater pilgrimage is the Day of Arafah. He meant that whoever catches the Day of Arafah until the rising of the dawn from the Day of Sacrifice has indeed caught the pilgrimage, and whoever misses that has missed the pilgrimage. Hence, he considered the night of Arafah as a standard for what is before it and what is after it. The evidence for this is that whoever catches the night of Sacrifice until the rising of the dawn has indeed caught the pilgrimage, and it suffices for him from Arafah.
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The Commander of the Believers (peace be upon him) said: The greater pilgrimage is the Day of Sacrifice.
So, travel freely in the land for four months

And they are twenty days from Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, Safar, the month of Rabi' al-Awwal, and ten days from the month of Rabi' al-Akhir. If the greater pilgrimage were on the Day of Arafah, the free travel would have been four months and one day.
And (it is) an announcement from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater pilgrimage
And I was the announcement among the people.

Then I said to him: What is the meaning of this phrase 'the greater pilgrimage'? He said: It was only named the greater because it was a year in which both the Muslims and the polytheists performed pilgrimage, and the polytheists did not perform pilgrimage after that year.
ai.seo_question: What is the definition of the greater pilgrimage (Hajj al-Akbar) according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) refutes the common view of Ibn Abbas by establishing the Day of Sacrifice as the 'Greater Pilgrimage,' supported by the four-month period of security in Surah At-Tawbah and his own role as the announcer of the verse. Historically, the term 'Akbar' signifies the final year when polytheists ceased performing Hajj, marking a transition in Islamic ritual authority. This distinction highlights the Shia emphasis on the specific timing and the Prophet's family's interpretive authority over communal practices.
